intro: Japanese rarely states a guess as a bare fact; it marks where the guess comes from and how sure you are. Two questions sort this whole group. Source: did you see it yourself (stem + そう), work it out from your own evidence (ようだ / みたいだ), or hear it from someone (plain form + そうだ, らしい)? Certainty: might (かもしれない), probably (でしょう / だろう), should be by logic (はずだ), must be (に違いない / に決まっている).

skills.rule: Verb ます-stem or adjective stem + そう means 'looks as if' or 'looks about to': 降りそう, おいしそう, 元気そう; いい and ない become よさそう and なさそう.
skills.explain:
This そう describes your immediate impression from what is in front of you, before you have checked: a cake that looks delicious (おいしそう), a sky that looks like rain (降りそう), a shelf that looks about to fall (倒れそう). With a verb it usually means 'about to happen', often with 今にも.

Form: drop い from i-adjectives (高そう), use na-adjectives as they are (静かそう), use the ます-stem of verbs (降りそう). Two exceptions: いい becomes よさそう, ない becomes なさそう (おいしくなさそう). It works like a na-adjective: おいしそうなケーキ, 楽しそうに遊ぶ. The negative of a verb is 降りそうにない or 降りそうもない.

It does not attach to nouns: 'he looks like a student' is 学生のようだ or 学生みたいだ, never 学生そう. And do not use it for what is plainly visible as a fact: a red flower is 赤い, not 赤そう.
patterns: [i-adj stem] そう(だ) · おいしそう
[na-adj stem] そう(だ) · 元気そう
[verb ます-stem] そう(だ) · 降りそう
よい → よさそう · ない → なさそう

examples.jp: このケーキ、おいし{そう}ですね。
examples.en: This cake looks delicious.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんは元気[げんき]{そう}でした。
examples.en: Mr Tanaka looked well.

examples.jp: 空[そら]が暗[くら]い。雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り{そう}だ。
examples.en: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.jp: 子[こ]どもたちが楽[たの]し{そう}に遊[あそ]んでいる。
examples.en: The children are playing and look like they're having fun.

examples.jp: この本棚[ほんだな]は今[いま]にも倒[たお]れ{そう}です。
examples.en: This bookcase looks as if it could fall over at any moment.

contrast.note: Hearsay そう follows the full plain form: おいしいそうだ = 'I hear it's delicious'. Stem + そう, おいしそうだ, = 'it looks delicious'. The stem is the signal.
ようだ is a judgement from evidence (the lights are off, so he seems to have left). そう is the first impression of what you are looking at, and it cannot follow a noun.

mistakes.bad: 写真[しゃしん]で見[み]ると、このホテルはいい{そう}ですね。
mistakes.good: 写真[しゃしん]で見[み]ると、このホテルはよさ{そう}ですね。
mistakes.note: You are judging from the photo, so you need 'looks good': いい becomes よさそう. いいそうです means 'I hear it's good'.

mistakes.bad: あの人[ひと]は学生[がくせい]{そう}です。
mistakes.good: あの人[ひと]は学生[がくせい]{みたい}です。
mistakes.note: Looks-like そう never follows a noun; use みたい or のよう.

skills.tip: Chopped stem (おいし-, 降り-, 静か-) + そう = I'm looking at it. Full plain form (おいしい, 降る, 静かだ) + そう = someone told me.

skills.rule: Full plain form + そうだ passes on what you heard or read: 降るそうだ, 高いそうだ, 静かだそうだ, 学生だそうだ.
skills.explain:
This そう reports information that came from someone else: the forecast, the news, a friend. You add nothing of your own; you are the messenger. Name the source with 〜によると or 〜の話では.

Form: the complete plain form goes in front, in any tense: 行くそうだ, 行かないそうだ, 行ったそうだ, 高いそうだ. Nouns and na-adjectives keep だ: 医者だそうだ, 静かだそうだ. Never put ます before it (×来ますそうです); politeness goes on the end: 来るそうです.

The そうだ itself does not change: there is no そうな + noun, no そうだった, and no そうではない. To report a negative, make the reported clause negative: 来ないそうです. Watch the pair 高そうだ ('looks expensive') and 高いそうだ ('I hear it's expensive'): only the full い form marks hearsay.
patterns: [plain verb / i-adj, any tense] そうだ · 降るそうだ, 高かったそうだ
[noun / na-adj] だそうだ · 医者だそうだ
[source] によると / の話では 〜そうだ

examples.jp: 天気予報[てんきよほう]によると、明日[あした]は雨[あめ]が降[ふ]る{そう}です。
examples.en: According to the forecast, it will rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんは来月[らいげつ]結婚[けっこん]する{そう}です。
examples.en: I hear Mr Tanaka is getting married next month.

examples.jp: あの店[みせ]のラーメンはとてもおいしい{そう}だよ。
examples.en: Apparently the ramen at that shop is really good.

examples.jp: 山田[やまだ]さんのお父[とう]さんは医者[いしゃ]だ{そう}です。
examples.en: I hear Ms Yamada's father is a doctor.

examples.jp: ニュースによると、駅前[えきまえ]に新[あたら]しい図書館[としょかん]ができた{そう}だ。
examples.en: According to the news, a new library has opened in front of the station.

contrast.note: Stem + そう is your own visual impression: おもしろそう = 'looks interesting'. Full form + そう is a report: おもしろいそう = 'I hear it's interesting'.
そうだ repeats what you were told, plainly. らしい also rests on what you heard but adds distance and doubt: 'apparently, so people say'.

mistakes.bad: 兄[あに]によると、あの映画[えいが]はおもしろ{そう}です。
mistakes.good: 兄[あに]によると、あの映画[えいが]はおもしろい{そう}です。
mistakes.note: Your brother told you, so it is hearsay: keep the full い form.

mistakes.bad: 鈴木[すずき]さんの趣味[しゅみ]は釣[つ]り{そう}です。
mistakes.good: 鈴木[すずき]さんの趣味[しゅみ]は釣[つ]りだ{そう}です。
mistakes.note: After a noun, hearsay needs だ: 釣りだそうです.

skills.tip: Could you add 'they say' in English? Then the full plain form goes before そう, with だ after nouns.

skills.rule: Plain form + ようだ (formal) or みたいだ (casual) means 'it seems' from your own evidence, and also 'like' in comparisons: 帰ったようだ, 夢のようだ, 夢みたいだ.
skills.explain:
ようだ is a conclusion you draw yourself from clues: the lights are off, so he seems to have gone home; my throat hurts, so I seem to have caught a cold. It is softer than stating the fact. みたいだ means the same and is the everyday spoken form.

It also makes comparisons: まるで夢のようだ ('it's like a dream'), 日本人のように話す ('speaks like a Japanese person'). Before a noun it becomes ような / みたいな; before a verb, ように / みたいに.

The forms differ. ようだ takes the noun modifying form: 行くようだ, 高いようだ, 静かなようだ, 学生のようだ. みたいだ attaches directly to nouns and na-adjectives: 学生みたい, 静かみたい, never 学生のみたい or 静かなみたい.
patterns: [plain verb / i-adj] ようだ / みたいだ
[na-adj] なようだ / [na-adj] みたいだ
[noun] のようだ / [noun] みたいだ
まるで [noun] のような / みたいな [noun]

examples.jp: 誰[だれ]もいない{みたい}ですね。
examples.en: It looks like nobody's here.

examples.jp: 風邪[かぜ]をひいた{みたい}。のどが痛[いた]い。
examples.en: I think I've caught a cold. My throat hurts.

examples.jp: 電気[でんき]が消[き]えている。田中[たなか]さんはもう帰[かえ]った{よう}だ。
examples.en: The lights are off. Mr Tanaka seems to have gone home already.

examples.jp: 夢[ゆめ]の{よう}な一日[いちにち]でした。
examples.en: It was a day like a dream.

examples.jp: ジョンさんは日本人[にほんじん]の{よう}に日本語[にほんご]を話[はな]します。
examples.en: John speaks Japanese like a Japanese person.

contrast.note: Stem + そう is a first visual impression or 'about to happen'. ようだ is a reasoned judgement and works with nouns: 学生のようだ, never 学生そう.

ようだ rests on your own evidence (what you see, hear, feel). らしい rests mainly on what others say or on indirect signs, and sounds detached; for what you feel in your own body, みたい / ようだ is the normal choice: のどが痛い、風邪をひいたみたい.
はずだ is an expectation from known facts before you see the result ('it should be'). ようだ comes from signs you are observing now.

mistakes.bad: 部長[ぶちょう]は今日[きょう]休[やす]みの{みたい}です。
mistakes.good: 部長[ぶちょう]は今日[きょう]休[やす]み{みたい}です。
mistakes.note: みたい attaches straight to a noun; の belongs to のよう.

mistakes.bad: この町[まち]は静[しず]か{よう}です。
mistakes.good: この町[まち]は静[しず]かな{よう}です。
mistakes.note: ようだ needs な after a na-adjective and の after a noun.

skills.tip: Can you point to the clue you are reasoning from? ようだ / みたい. Casual speech: みたい, no の, no な.

skills.rule: Plain form + らしい means 'apparently', a guess based mainly on what you heard; noun + らしい means 'typical of, as a real N should be': 辞めるらしい, 春らしい.
skills.explain:
Use 1, hearsay guess: 鈴木さんは会社を辞めるらしい ('apparently Suzuki is quitting'). The information came from outside, and the speaker keeps some distance from it: it is not their own judgement and they do not vouch for it. Form: plain verb or i-adjective; nouns and na-adjectives attach directly, with no だ: 学生らしい, 静からしい.

Use 2, typical of: noun + らしい is an i-adjective meaning 'having the true qualities of N': 春らしい天気 (real spring weather), 男らしい, 彼らしい ('so like him'). It is usually praise for something that is N and behaves as N should. For something that is not N but resembles it, use みたい or っぽい: an adult who talks 子どもみたい, not 子どもらしい.

学生らしい can therefore mean 'seems to be a student' or 'student-like'; context decides.
patterns: [plain verb / i-adj] らしい · 辞めるらしい
[noun / na-adj] らしい · 休みらしい (apparently)
[noun] らしい [noun] / らしく · 春らしい天気 (typical)

examples.jp: 鈴木[すずき]さんは会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]める{らしい}よ。
examples.en: Apparently Mr Suzuki is quitting his job.

examples.jp: 駅前[えきまえ]のパン屋[や]は来月[らいげつ]閉[し]まる{らしい}です。
examples.en: Apparently the bakery in front of the station is closing next month.

examples.jp: 今年[ことし]の夏[なつ]はかなり暑[あつ]くなる{らしい}。
examples.en: Apparently this summer is going to be pretty hot.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は春[はる]{らしい}暖[あたた]かい日[ひ]ですね。
examples.en: It's a warm, truly spring-like day today.

examples.jp: 最後[さいご]まであきらめないのは、彼[かれ]{らしい}ね。
examples.en: Not giving up until the end is so like him.

contrast.note: そうだ passes the message on as told, often with the source named. らしい marks it as a rumour or an inference from what you heard.
ようだ is your own reading of evidence. In the 'typical' sense, みたい means 'like something it is not' (子どもみたい about an adult); らしい means 'a true example of' (子どもらしい about a child).

mistakes.bad: 大人[おとな]なのに、子[こ]ども{らしい}ことを言[い]わないで。
mistakes.good: 大人[おとな]なのに、子[こ]ども{みたいな}ことを言[い]わないで。
mistakes.note: An adult acting like a child is 'like' something they are not: みたい. らしい would praise a real child.

mistakes.bad: 課長[かちょう]は明日[あした]休[やす]みだ{らしい}。
mistakes.good: 課長[かちょう]は明日[あした]休[やす]み{らしい}。
mistakes.note: Nouns and na-adjectives attach to らしい directly, with no だ: 休みらしい, 静からしい.

skills.tip: 'Word on the street is...' or 'a true N': らしい. Your own clues: ようだ / みたい.

skills.rule: でしょう / だろう is 'probably' (a fairly confident guess); かもしれない is 'might' (a real possibility, often 50 percent or less). Both follow the plain form, with no だ after nouns.
skills.explain:
でしょう is the polite form, だろう the plain one. They give the speaker's guess about the future or about something they cannot check: 明日は晴れるでしょう. They pair with たぶん and きっと. Spoken with a rising tone, でしょう? / だろう? asks for agreement: 'right?'

かもしれない (polite かもしれません) only says the possibility exists. It pairs with もしかしたら / もしかすると. 遅れるでしょう means you expect the delay; 遅れるかもしれない only means it could happen.

Form for both: plain verb or i-adjective in any tense (来ないでしょう, 高かったかもしれない); nouns and na-adjectives attach directly: 雨でしょう, 学生かもしれない, 静かだろう. Never 雨だでしょう, and never a ます form before them. Do not use でしょう for your own decisions; say つもりです or と思います.
patterns: [plain form] でしょう / だろう
[plain form] かもしれない / かもしれません
[noun / na-adj] でしょう / かもしれない (no だ)

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は晴[は]れる{でしょう}。
examples.en: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.

examples.jp: この問題[もんだい]は子[こ]どもには難[むずか]しい{でしょう}。
examples.en: This problem is probably difficult for children.

examples.jp: 道[みち]が混[こ]んでいるから、たぶん間[ま]に合[あ]わない{だろう}。
examples.en: The roads are busy, so we probably won't make it in time.

examples.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]が止[と]まっているので、少[すこ]し遅[おく]れる{かもしれません}。
examples.en: The trains have stopped, so I might be a little late.

examples.jp: もしかしたら、あの人[ひと]が新[あたら]しい先生[せんせい]{かもしれない}。
examples.en: That person might be the new teacher.

contrast.note: はずだ rests on facts or arrangements ('it should arrive, I paid for next-day delivery'). でしょう is a general guess with no stated basis.
らしい and hearsay そうだ come from what others said. でしょう and かもしれない are your own estimate.
に違いない is near certainty ('must be'). If you are not sure, it is too strong; use でしょう or かもしれない.

mistakes.bad: 午後[ごご]は雨[あめ]だ{でしょう}。
mistakes.good: 午後[ごご]は雨[あめ]{でしょう}。
mistakes.note: Nouns and na-adjectives attach directly: no だ before でしょう or かもしれない.

mistakes.bad: 来週[らいしゅう]は忙[いそが]しくなります{かもしれません}。
mistakes.good: 来週[らいしゅう]は忙[いそが]しくなる{かもしれません}。
mistakes.note: The plain form goes first; politeness goes only on the end.

skills.tip: Would you bet on it? でしょう. Only that it's possible? かもしれない. Noun in front? No だ.

skills.rule: はずだ is 'should be, is supposed to be' by logic or known facts; はずがない is 'cannot possibly be'; はずだった is 'was supposed to (but didn't)'.
skills.explain:
はずだ states what you expect because of something you know: a schedule, a rule, someone's history. 荷物は今日届くはずだ: you know it was sent express. The basis is facts, not hope or feeling.

はずがない (also はずはない) denies a possibility outright: あの人がうそをつくはずがない ('he can't possibly be lying'). It is stronger than ないはずだ, which only says 'I expect not': 来ないはずだ = he is not supposed to come. はずだった means the expectation failed: 九時に着くはずだった (it was supposed to arrive at nine).

Form: noun modifying form. Verbs and i-adjectives plain (行くはず, 高いはず), na-adjective + な (静かなはず), noun + の (休みのはず). It is not 'ought to' in the moral sense; that is べきだ. And for a plan you decide yourself, use つもりだ.
patterns: [plain verb / i-adj] はずだ
[na-adj] なはずだ · [noun] のはずだ
[plain form] はずがない / はずはない
[plain form] はずだった

examples.jp: 荷物[にもつ]は今日[きょう]届[とど]く{はず}です。
examples.en: The parcel should arrive today.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は日曜日[にちようび]だから、銀行[ぎんこう]は休[やす]みの{はず}だ。
examples.en: It's Sunday, so the bank should be closed.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんは三年[さんねん]日本[にほん]に住[す]んでいたから、日本語[にほんご]が話[はな]せる{はず}です。
examples.en: Ms Tanaka lived in Japan for three years, so she should be able to speak Japanese.

examples.jp: 鍵[かぎ]はかばんに入[い]れた{はず}なのに、見[み]つからない。
examples.en: I'm sure I put the key in my bag, but I can't find it.

examples.jp: あんなにまじめな人[ひと]がうそをつく{はずがない}。
examples.en: Someone that honest can't possibly be lying.

examples.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]は九時[くじ]に着[つ]く{はずだった}が、事故[じこ]で遅[おく]れた。
examples.en: The train was supposed to arrive at nine, but it was delayed by an accident.

contrast.note: べきだ is moral duty, 'ought to': 約束は守るべきだ. はずだ is an expectation about what is or will be the case.
わけだ explains a fact you now understand ('so that's why'). はずだ predicts something not yet confirmed.
つもりだ is your own intention. はずだ is an expectation based on facts, usually about other people or events.

mistakes.bad: 健康[けんこう]のために、野菜[やさい]をもっと食[た]べる{はず}だ。
mistakes.good: 健康[けんこう]のために、野菜[やさい]をもっと食[た]べる{べき}だ。
mistakes.note: 'You ought to eat more vegetables' is a duty or advice: べきだ.

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]は祝日[しゅくじつ]だから、学校[がっこう]は休[やす]み{はず}だ。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]は祝日[しゅくじつ]だから、学校[がっこう]は休[やす]みの{はず}だ。
mistakes.note: A noun needs の before はず.

skills.tip: Can you finish with 'because I know that...'? はずだ. 'No way!'? はずがない.

skills.rule: に違いない and に決まっている mean 'must be, it's certain'; they follow the plain form, with nouns and na-adjectives attached directly (うそに違いない).
skills.explain:
Both express near certainty, the strongest step on the scale かもしれない, でしょう, はずだ, に違いない. に違いない (polite に違いありません) is the speaker's firm conviction, often reached by intuition or from strong signs: 誰かいるに違いない. It is common in writing and careful speech.

に決まっている (casual 決まってる) is conversational and emphatic: 'obviously, of course'. It can sound pushy or dismissive, especially about other people: そんなのうそに決まってる. Do not use it to someone senior.

Form: plain verb or i-adjective, any tense (来たに違いない); nouns and na-adjectives attach directly, without だ: 犯人に違いない, 無理に決まっている. A negative clause in front is fine (来ないに違いない, 'he surely won't come'), but to deny a possibility outright ('it can't be') the normal tools are はずがない and わけがない.
patterns: [plain verb / i-adj] に違いない / に決まっている
[noun / na-adj] に違いない / に決まっている (no だ)

examples.jp: 電気[でんき]がついている。誰[だれ]かいる{に違[ちが]いない}。
examples.en: The light is on. There must be someone in.

examples.jp: この財布[さいふ]は田中[たなか]さんのもの{に違[ちが]いない}。
examples.en: This wallet must be Mr Tanaka's.

examples.jp: あんなに練習[れんしゅう]したのだから、合格[ごうかく]する{に違[ちが]いありません}。
examples.en: After all that practice, you're sure to pass.

examples.jp: そんな話[はなし]、うそ{に決[き]まっている}よ。
examples.en: A story like that is obviously a lie.

examples.jp: 一人[ひとり]で夜[よる]の山[やま]に行[い]くなんて、危[あぶ]ない{に決[き]まっている}。
examples.en: Going into the mountains alone at night is obviously dangerous.

contrast.note: かもしれない is mere possibility; に違いない is the opposite end of the scale, near certainty.
はずだ reasons from known facts ('given the timetable, it should be here'). に違いない is a firm conviction, often from intuition or circumstantial signs.

contrast.vs: はずがない / わけがない
contrast.note: These are certainty that something is NOT so. に違いない and に決まっている only assert that something IS so.

mistakes.bad: あの声[こえ]は佐藤[さとう]さんだ{に違[ちが]いない}。
mistakes.good: あの声[こえ]は佐藤[さとう]さん{に違[ちが]いない}。
mistakes.note: No だ between a noun and に違いない.

mistakes.bad: 田中[たなか]さんはもう帰[かえ]りました{に違[ちが]いない}。
mistakes.good: 田中[たなか]さんはもう帰[かえ]った{に違[ちが]いない}。
mistakes.note: The plain form goes in front; politeness goes only on the end: 帰ったに違いありません.

skills.tip: Ninety-nine percent sure it IS so? に違いない (written, careful) or に決まってる (spoken, 'obviously').

skills.rule: Ask: was I told? did I see it just now? did I reason it from clues? am I comparing? The answer picks hearsay そう / らしい, stem + そう, ようだ / みたい, or noun + らしい / みたい.
skills.explain:
Q1. Did the information come from someone else? If you simply pass it on, full plain form + そうだ (降るそうだ, 学生だそうだ). If it is a rumour you only half vouch for, らしい (降るらしい).

Q2. Is it your first impression of something in front of you, or something about to happen? Stem + そう: おいしそう, 降りそう. Check: is the word before そう chopped? If a noun is in front, そう is impossible.

Q3. Are you reasoning from your own clues: sights, sounds, your body? ようだ (formal) or みたいだ (casual): 帰ったようだ, 風邪みたい.

Q4. Is it a comparison? Like something it is not (まるで夢のよう, 子どもみたい): ようだ / みたい. A true example of N (春らしい, 子どもらしい): らしい.

Form check with a noun: 学生だそうだ, 学生のようだ, 学生みたいだ, 学生らしい; never 学生そうだ.
patterns: told, passed on → [plain form] そうだ
heard, unconfirmed → [plain form] らしい
seen now / about to → [stem] そうだ
own clues → ようだ (formal) / みたいだ (casual)
like X → ようだ / みたい · a true X → X らしい

examples.jp: 空[そら]が暗[くら]い。雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り{そう}だ。
examples.en: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.jp: 天気予報[てんきよほう]によると、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]る{そう}だ。
examples.en: According to the forecast, it's going to rain.

examples.jp: 道[みち]がぬれている。夜[よる]の間[あいだ]に雨[あめ]が降[ふ]った{よう}だ。
examples.en: The road is wet. It seems it rained during the night.

examples.jp: うわさでは、鈴木[すずき]さんは来月[らいげつ]引[ひ]っ越[こ]す{らしい}。
examples.en: Rumour has it that Mr Suzuki is moving next month.

examples.jp: あの人[ひと]、何[なに]か探[さが]している{みたい}だね。
examples.en: That person seems to be looking for something.

examples.jp: この子[こ]は笑[わら]い方[かた]がとても子[こ]ども{らしい}。
examples.en: This child laughs just the way a child should.

contrast.vs: 降りそう vs 降るそう
contrast.note: Same verb, different source: 降りそうだ (I see dark clouds) and 降るそうだ (the forecast said so). The stem means you see it; the full form means you were told.

contrast.vs: ようだ vs らしい
contrast.note: Wet road, so it rained: ようだ (my evidence; らしい is possible but sounds detached). A colleague said it rained at the coast: らしい (their evidence).

contrast.vs: 子どもみたい vs 子どもらしい
contrast.note: About an adult: 子どもみたい (childish, like what he is not). About a child: 子どもらしい (a proper child, praise).

mistakes.bad: ニュースによると、来年[らいねん]は税金[ぜいきん]が上[あ]がり{そう}です。
mistakes.good: ニュースによると、来年[らいねん]は税金[ぜいきん]が上[あ]がる{そう}です。
mistakes.note: によると names a source, so it is hearsay: full plain form + そう.

mistakes.bad: 窓[まど]から見[み]ると、外[そと]は寒[さむ]い{そう}だ。
mistakes.good: 窓[まど]から見[み]ると、外[そと]は寒[さむ]{そう}だ。
mistakes.note: You are looking out of the window yourself: stem + そう (寒そう).

mistakes.bad: あの人[ひと]は先生[せんせい]{そう}だ。
mistakes.good: あの人[ひと]は先生[せんせい]{みたい}だ。
mistakes.note: Looks-like そう never follows a noun; judge from clues with みたい or のよう.

skills.tip: Told → full form そう. Seen → stem そう. Clues → よう / みたい. Rumour or 'a true N' → らしい.
